newsitem.title: JAPAN: Policeman informed Japan cult on police activity.
newsitem.headline: Policeman informed Japan cult on police activity.

text.p: A policeman who officials say confessed to shooting Japan's national police chief routinely informed on police activities to the cult accused of the Tokyo subway gas attack, a cult member said on Wednesday.

Yoshihiro Inoue, on trial for his alleged involvement in the subway gassing last year, testified in the Tokyo District Court that he learned of police probes into his cult through the officer, who was also a cult member.

Earlier, Inoue, who was one of guru Shoko Asahara's top lieutenants, told investigators he was in contact with the same policeman since he started heading the cult's "intelligence" division in 1994, newspaper reports said.

Government officials said last week that a 31-year-old policeman who belonged to the Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect) was being questioned after confessing to shooting and nearly killing Japan's chief police officer last March at the height of the probe into the sect.

Officials said that in his confession, the officer said he acted on orders of cult members to disrupt police probes into the March 20, 1995, subway gas attack, which killed 12 people and harmed 6,000.
The investigators, however, failed to report the confession to higher authority, leading to media charges that the local police covered it up to avoid embarrassment.
A senior Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department officer in charge of the investigation was replaced on Tuesday.
The confession came to light only after Japanese media followed up an anonymous letter accusing local police of a cover-up.
Sect guru Shoko Asahara and about 100 of his cult followers are on trial for the gas attack and other crimes. Asahara is scheduled to appear in court next week.

But media reports quoted judicial sources as saying they were worried they may have to cancel next week's trial sessions as Asahara was moved back to a padded cell last week after repeated violent outbursts.
Media reports quoted prosecutors as saying that Asahara was merely trying to prolong his trial.
